nuggets.title: Bad upstream partition blocked entire nightly load

scenario.symptoms: Warehouse load failed at 2 a.m. because one Kafka partition had corrupt JSON for three hours. Downstream marts empty for morning dashboards.
scenario.interviewerSetup: ETL aborts whole batch on first poison message without quarantine or circuit breaker per partition.

incident.headline: All-or-nothing batch fails on single poison record

agenda.goal: Explain how the system physically prevents bad data from reaching downstream consumers.
agenda.opener: One bad partition stopped the whole pipeline—the ingest path is highlighted. How do you isolate failure?

evidence.strong: Integrates directly with the pipeline orchestrator using a circuit-breaker pattern, failing the DAG run based on block-level severity rules.
evidence.adequate: Mentions stopping the pipeline but relies on polling or manual intervention to halt downstream tasks.
evidence.weak: Runs checks on a schedule after data is written, relying on alerts rather than prevention.

misconceptions.pattern: Running checks asynchronously after the publish step completes.
misconceptions.challenge: If a dashboard queries the table exactly one minute after your pipeline finishes, how did your asynchronous check protect it?

probes: How do we distinguish between a check that should halt the pipeline and one that just warns the owner?
If the check takes 20 minutes to run, how does that impact the upstream pipeline?
hints: Think about intermediate tables or staging areas.
How can the framework signal the orchestrator to fail the current job?
agenda.referenceFix: Per-partition circuit breakers, quarantine bad records with alerts, continue healthy partitions, replay quarantine after fix, and SLAs on loaded row counts.

nuggets.title: Renamed column broke report with no lineage alert

scenario.symptoms: CEO dashboard showed blank revenue for a day after an engineer renamed a field in the raw layer. No alert fired because downstream job silently null-filled.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Lineage graph exists but breaking schema changes don't trigger consumers; jobs coerce missing fields to null.

incident.headline: Schema change without consumer contract notification

agenda.goal: Design a lineage data model and collection strategy to trace incident impact.
agenda.opener: A rename blanked revenue—the lineage and contract path is highlighted. How do you catch this pre-deploy?

evidence.strong: Uses a graph model for datasets, jobs, and dashboards. Discusses parsing query logs vs. explicit API emission for lineage metadata.
evidence.adequate: Mentions a database table tracking source-to-destination pairs and recursively querying it.
evidence.weak: Assumes lineage is magically known or relies entirely on manual documentation by developers.

misconceptions.pattern: Relying on teams to manually declare all downstream consumers.
misconceptions.challenge: If a new team builds a dashboard on top of our table without telling us, how does our system know they exist?

probes: What kind of database is best suited for traversing multiple levels of downstream dependencies?
How do we capture lineage from a complex SQL transformation?
hints: SQL queries contain `FROM` and `INSERT INTO` statements that can be parsed.
Consider graph databases for fast traversal of dependency chains.
agenda.referenceFix: Contract tests on producers, block deploy breaking dependents, lineage-driven notifications, and non-null assertions on critical metrics.

nuggets.title: Null rate spike unnoticed for a week

scenario.symptoms: Customer age field became 90% null after a mobile bug but quality checks only ran monthly. Segmentation models degraded silently.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Profiling job weekly; no streaming checks on null rate or distribution drift.

agenda.goal: Handle statistical anomaly detection and alert fatigue for metrics like row count or null rates.
agenda.opener: A mobile bug nulled a column for days—the profiling path is highlighted. How do you detect faster?

evidence.strong: Stores time-series metrics and uses statistical methods (like z-scores or moving averages) that account for seasonality and trend.
evidence.adequate: Uses a time-series database and static thresholds or simple percentage-based rules.
evidence.weak: Hardcodes expected row counts or ignores historical trends entirely.

misconceptions.pattern: Using static rules for all anomaly detection.
misconceptions.challenge: If our business grows 10% every month, won't a static volume rule break constantly?

probes: Where are you storing the historical check results to calculate these trends?
If a team gets too many false positives, what mechanism allows them to tune the alerts?
hints: We need to look at what the metric was last week or last month, not just yesterday.
Consider using a time-series database to track metric history.
agenda.referenceFix: Streaming expectations on null rate and cardinality, anomaly detection on profiles, block releases when checks fail, tie to owner dashboards.

nuggets.title: Producer shipped extra enum value crashing consumer

scenario.symptoms: Payments pipeline stalled because a new status enum value appeared without consumer update. Spark job threw enum parse exceptions for 6 hours.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Avro schema marked compatible but semantic enum extension not coordinated; consumers use strict pattern match.

incident.headline: Backward incompatible semantic change passed registry

agenda.goal: Define how schema expectations are managed between data producers and consumers.
agenda.opener: A new enum value stopped Spark—the contract path is highlighted. How do you evolve safely?

evidence.strong: Proposes declarative data contracts stored in a registry, enforced at deployment or ingestion time before data enters the warehouse.
evidence.adequate: Detects the schema change after the fact and alerts the downstream owner.
evidence.weak: Relies purely on the data warehouse throwing an error when the query is run.

misconceptions.pattern: Treating schema drift only as a data check rather than a CI/CD or registry problem.
misconceptions.challenge: If we wait until the pipeline runs to catch the dropped column, haven't we already broken the contract?

probes: Where are these contracts defined, and who owns them?
Can we catch a schema violation before the pipeline even executes?
hints: Think about integrating schema checks into the CI/CD pipeline of the upstream service.
A central schema registry can hold the agreed-upon structure.
agenda.referenceFix: Consumer-driven contracts, semantic compatibility tests, default unknown handling, coordinated rollout with feature flags, and DLQ replay after fix.

nuggets.title: Quality scan times out on skewed partition

scenario.symptoms: Daily quality scan missed SLA because one huge tenant partition dominated scan time; other partitions finished in minutes.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Scan job uses single thread per table without salting or parallel split on tenant key.

incident.headline: Unpartitioned scan skewed on hot tenant

agenda.goal: Design the storage layer for framework metadata, historical metrics, and lineage data.
agenda.opener: Quality job timed out on one giant tenant—the scan path is highlighted. How do you scale checks?

evidence.strong: Splits storage appropriately: relational/document for configurations, time-series for metrics history, and graph for lineage.
evidence.adequate: Puts everything into a single relational database but correctly identifies indexing strategies.
evidence.weak: Stores framework configuration inside the analytical data warehouse directly, mixing data plane and control plane.

misconceptions.pattern: Using a relational DB for complex lineage traversal at scale.
misconceptions.challenge: If we have a lineage chain 15 levels deep, how does a standard SQL database perform on that query?

probes: What is the write-per-second volume for the metrics database during peak ETL hours?
How do you ensure fast reads for the incident dashboards?
hints: Lineage is inherently a network of connected nodes.
Millions of check results daily behave like metrics.
agenda.referenceFix: Split scans by partition key ranges, sample heavy tenants separately, adaptive parallelism, track per-partition duration, and incremental checks on deltas.
